title: India Pulled In $1.56 Billion in Data Centre Investment in Six Months. That Is Seven Times Last Year's Pace.
excerpt: Amazon just committed $13 billion more, HCLTech is building its own AI data centres, and AI spending is projected to grow 39 percent annually through 2030. India's digital infrastructure buildout is accelerating faster than anyone expected.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India attracted $1.56 billion in data centre investments in H1 2023, seven times last year's amount.
  • Amazon plans to invest an additional $13 billion in AI and cloud infrastructure in India.
  • HCLTech is building its own AI data centres, marking a shift in IT services strategy.
  • India's AI spending is projected to grow 39% annually through 2030, outpacing Southeast Asia.
  • NRI professionals are increasingly drawn back to India for high-demand tech roles.

Six months ago, India's data centre investment story was still largely about announcements and intentions. Now the money is arriving. Foreign investors poured $1.56 billion into India's data centre and digital infrastructure ecosystem in the first half of 2023, according to data tracked by Tracxn. That is nearly seven times the $111 million invested across the entire digital infrastructure ecosystem in the first half of 2022. Data centres alone attracted $738 million in foreign capital during the period. The biggest single deal was Airtel's Nxtra Data, the data centre arm of Bharti Airtel, which landed $710 million from global investors. But the broader trend is being driven by hyperscalers — Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and their peers — racing to build AI-ready compute capacity in one of the world's fastest-growing digital economies. This surge in investment not only signals robust economic growth but also creates significant opportunities for the Indian diaspora, from tech professionals considering relocation to investors looking for high-growth sectors. ## Amazon Goes Bigger Amazon made the most dramatic move. After CEO Andy Jassy met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, the company announced an additional $13 billion investment in India for AI and cloud infrastructure, taking its total planned spend between 2023 and 2030 to $48 billion. AWS will expand data centre capacity in Mumbai and Hyderabad, providing access to custom AI chips, managed AI services, and cloud developer tools. The numbers are staggering by any measure. Amazon's cumulative investments in India between 2010 and 2030 will exceed $88 billion. The company says it has digitised 12 million small businesses, enabled over $20 billion in e-commerce exports, and supported 2.8 million jobs in the country. For Indian Americans who built careers at Amazon and AWS — and there are tens of thousands — the India expansion creates a reverse funnel. Senior roles in cloud architecture, AI operations, and data centre engineering are opening in Hyderabad and Mumbai, and AWS is actively recruiting NRIs willing to relocate. The salary gap between US and India data centre roles, while still significant, is narrowing for senior technical positions, making these opportunities increasingly attractive for those seeking to contribute to India's tech boom. ## HCLTech Enters the Arena Perhaps the most unexpected development came from HCLTech. The IT services giant, fresh off a strong quarterly earnings report that included $171 million in AI revenue and a record $2.4 billion in new bookings, announced it will build its own AI data centres. CEO C. Vijayakumar framed the move as a play for India's sovereign AI ecosystem. "This will position us as a key enabler of India's sovereign AI ecosystem, expanding our presence in the fastest-growing market among largest economies," he said. HCL is already in advanced discussions with clients for committed consumption from day one. The move is unusual. IT services companies have historically rented compute capacity from hyperscalers rather than building their own infrastructure. HCLTech's decision signals that the margins in AI infrastructure — not just AI services — are attractive enough to justify the capital expenditure. It also reflects growing demand from Indian enterprises and government agencies that want AI infrastructure on sovereign soil, not in a foreign cloud region. This strategic shift by a major Indian tech player further solidifies the nation's position as a global data hub, potentially drawing more NRI talent and investment into the sector.

## The Numbers Behind the Boom IDC's Rajiv Ranjan, associate research director for cloud and data centres, expects India's AI spending to grow at a compound annual rate of 39 percent from 2023 to 2030. Public cloud spending is projected to expand at 23 percent over the same period. By 2028-2030, Ranjan estimates that 30 to 40 percent of AI deployments will take place outside the public cloud — in private data centres, edge locations, and sovereign facilities. India's data centre expansion is now outpacing growth in Southeast Asian markets including Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand. IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has said total data centre investments will exceed $200 billion, though he has not specified the timeline. This rapid growth underscores India's emergence as a global leader in digital infrastructure, a development that resonates deeply with the diaspora, many of whom maintain strong professional and financial ties to the homeland. ## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI investors, India's data centre buildout offers exposure through multiple channels. Bharti Airtel, which owns Nxtra, is publicly traded and its stock has benefited from the data centre narrative. The Nifty IT index, despite a rough 2023, contains companies like HCLTech that are pivoting toward infrastructure revenue. Real estate investment trusts focused on data centre properties are also emerging in India's capital markets, providing new avenues for diaspora capital. We've seen several NRI-led investment groups actively exploring these opportunities, leveraging their international experience to identify promising ventures. For Indian technologists in the US, the career calculus is shifting. A decade ago, returning to India meant accepting lower compensation for less interesting work. Today, building AI infrastructure in Hyderabad or Mumbai — for Amazon, Google, or HCLTech — is among the most technically demanding work available anywhere. The $1.56 billion that flowed into India in the first half of this year is not just capital. It is a statement about where the next generation of computing infrastructure will be built, and a clear invitation for the diaspora to be part of this transformative journey. We've heard stories of NRIs, like a former Google cloud architect now leading a team in Bengaluru, who are finding immense professional satisfaction and impact by contributing to India's digital future.
